text: Tap your phone with a glove... nothing. Tap it with a sausage... it works! Because your screen can't feel your finger at all. It feels your electricity. To see how, we have to take it apart.
Lift the layers apart. On top, tough glass. At the bottom, the display that makes the picture. And in between, a layer you can't even see.
It's a grid of see-through wires. Often made of indium tin oxide. It conducts like a metal, but you can see straight through it. Rows going one way. Columns going the other.
The chip sends a pulse down each row. At every crossing, a tiny electric field reaches over to the column. And the chip measures every crossing, again and again, many times a second.
Now, your finger. It's mostly salty water, so it conducts electricity. As it comes close, it steals part of that field.
The signal at that crossing drops. The chip sees the dip, and knows. A finger. Right here.
But your finger is wider than one crossing. So it dims a few at once. The chip compares how much each one dropped, and finds the exact centre, much finer than the grid.
Two fingers? Two dips. The chip tracks both at the same time. That's how pinch to zoom works.
A wool glove doesn't conduct. Your finger's charge never reaches the screen, so nothing changes. Touch screen gloves weave conductive thread into the fingertips.
Water conducts too. That's why raindrops can make a wet screen tap things on its own.
And the sausage? Salty, wet, and conductive. As far as your phone can tell, it's a finger.
Old screens worked differently. Two flexible layers had to be pushed together until they touched. That's why you had to press hard, often with a plastic stick.
Today, one light tap is all it takes. On Orbi Transfer, that tap locks your file, on your phone, before it leaves.
It reaches the other phone in about a second. No login, no app. And after thirty minutes, it burns.
Orbi Transfer dot com. Your screen doesn't feel your finger. It feels your electricity.
